title.en: Geography: Disaster Management: Responding to Disasters

text.en: Meena saw news of a flood on TV. "How can people stay safe?" she asked.

A disaster is a sudden event that causes great loss. Natural disasters include floods, cyclones, earthquakes, droughts and tsunamis, while man-made ones include fires and industrial accidents. Hazards become disasters when people are not prepared.
Disaster management has stages: mitigation (reducing risk), preparedness, response and recovery. Early warnings, evacuation plans, shelters and first aid save lives. In India the National Disaster Management Authority leads the effort.
Citizens should know safe places, keep an emergency kit and follow instructions. For earthquakes, drop, cover and hold; for floods move to higher ground. The 2004 tsunami in Tamil Nadu taught valuable lessons.

First, distinguish a hazard from a disaster. A hazard is a potentially dangerous event—like a cyclone forming over the Bay of Bengal—whereas a disaster happens when that hazard strikes a vulnerable community and causes severe loss.
Disasters are grouped into natural disasters—earthquakes, tsunamis, cyclones, floods, droughts and landslides—and human-made disasters such as industrial chemical leaks, fires and transport crashes.
Because Tamil Nadu has a long eastern coastline along the Bay of Bengal, coastal districts must stay especially prepared for tropical cyclones, storm surges and tsunamis.

board.text: Tamil Nadu coastal risks: cyclones & tsunamis

text.en: Disaster management follows a continuous four-phase cycle: Mitigation (reducing risks before a hazard), Preparedness (planning and drills), Response (rescue during crisis), and Recovery (rebuilding safer).
In India, the Disaster Management Act of 2005 set up a three-tier structure: NDMA led by the Prime Minister, SDMA led by the Chief Minister, and DDMA led by the District Collector.
The National Disaster Response Force, or NDRF, along with State Disaster Response Forces and local volunteers, conducts specialised rescue and relief operations.
Now let us learn exact life-saving actions for each major disaster. During an earthquake, remember three words: Drop, Cover and Hold On!
Drop to your hands and knees, take cover under a sturdy desk or table away from windows and shelves, and hold on until shaking stops. Never use elevators during an earthquake.
If you are outdoors during a quake, move calmly to an open ground away from buildings, electric poles, trees and overhead wires.
Next, tsunami safety. A strong coastal earthquake or sudden strange recession of seawater exposing the sea floor is a natural tsunami warning—move immediately to high ground inland!

board.text: Tsunami clue: sea pulls back -> go to high ground

text.en: Never go to the beach to watch incoming tsunami waves; subsequent waves are often much taller and faster than the first.

board.text: Never watch tsunami waves from the shore

text.en: For cyclones, listen to official India Meteorological Department alerts, secure loose roofs and windows, switch off electrical mains if flooding begins, and evacuate early to cyclone shelters.

board.text: Cyclone: follow IMD alerts & use shelters

text.en: During floods, never walk or ride through moving floodwater—just fifteen centimetres of fast water can knock an adult down, and hidden drains or live wires may lie underneath.

board.text: Floods: never wade through moving water

text.en: For fire emergencies, remember the PASS rule for fire extinguishers (Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep), stay low under rising smoke, and if clothes catch fire: Stop, Drop and Roll!

board.text: Fire: stay low; clothes on fire -> Stop, Drop, Roll

text.en: In hilly districts like the Nilgiris during heavy rain, watch for landslide signs—cracks in slopes, tilting trees or muddy streams—and move away from steep hillsides promptly.

board.text: Landslides: watch slope cracks in heavy rain

text.en: Every family and school should pack an Emergency Go-Kit: drinking water, dry food, torch with extra batteries, first-aid kit, whistle, essential medicines and copies of ID cards in a waterproof pouch.
Schools hold regular mock drills so students know assembly points, exit routes and buddy systems without panicking during a real emergency.
In a stampede or crowded festival, stay calm, avoid pushing, keep arms bent across your chest to protect breathing space, and move diagonally toward the outer edge of the crowd.

board.text: Crowd safety: stay calm, move diagonally out

text.en: After any disaster, drink only boiled or chlorinated water to prevent water-borne diseases like cholera and typhoid, and stay clear of damaged buildings and fallen power lines.

board.text: Post-disaster: safe water & avoid fallen wires

text.en: Community first responders—trained youth, neighbours and local panchayats—are always the very first to reach victims before outside teams arrive.
To review any disaster scenario, match the hazard to its immediate action: Earthquake -> Drop/Cover/Hold; Tsunami -> High ground; Fire -> Stay low / Stop-Drop-Roll; Cyclone -> Shelter & IMD alerts.
Preparedness turns fear into calm action—a prepared student can protect themselves, their family and their entire school.

problem.en: While visiting a coastal town, you feel a strong earthquake and notice the sea suddenly pulling far back from the shore. What is happening, and what must you do immediately?

text.en: Recognise the natural warning sign.

why.en: A coastal earthquake followed by rapid sea withdrawal is a classic warning of an approaching tsunami.

text.en: Choose the immediate life-saving action.

why.en: Do not wait for sirens or film the beach—move immediately inland and uphill to high ground or a designated multi-storey cyclone/tsunami shelter.

text.en: Stay safe until official clearance.

why.en: Remain on high ground until authorities announce all-clear, because later tsunami waves can be larger than the first.

prompt.en: A friend says Disasters cannot be reduced by preparation. How will you reply?
